items.content:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.content:
@heyshrutimishra LLMs accumulate a lot of declarative knowledge.
That's how they can answer a large number of questions. 
That's also why they require so many parameters and hence so much memory. 

But one can replace the accumulation of knowledge by *understanding*
That what JEPA world models do. 
That's one reason they can be useful with considerably less memory and training data  than LLMs. 

This paper merely shows that the underlying similarity structure of the data, whether text or image (e.g. co-occurence of words in text or objects in images) uniquely determines the shape of the representation point cloud, when the encoder is trained trained with a common anti-collapse criterion like SIGReg or VCReg (not by reconstruction).

items.content:
My vlog today was fully edited by Claude Code with Opus 5.5!

I copied the video clips from my DJI to a folder, then opened Claude Code in it and asked it to edit it into a 10 minute vlog

I made a few adjustments but not a lot

It transcribed everything I said with mlx-whisper (Whisper large-v3-turbo running on my MacBook Pro's GPU through Apple's MLX)

It pulled video frames every few seconds into grid images (contact sheets), so Claude could see what's in each clip

It used SpeechBrain ECAPA (a voice-matching model) to figure out what was my voice from other people

It then made thumbnails with OpenCV with YuNet's face detector

The edit itself is a list of cuts in a JSON file: which clip, start time, end time, Claude then picked the pieces by reading the transcripts and looking at the frame grids by itself

I added on screen captions for X and on YouTube for the first minute with Pillow (Python's image library)

P.S. I didn't ask for any of this, and I didn't know any of this until @thesamparr just asked me how I edited it

All I asked for was "Claude can you edit these clips into a 10 minute vlog for X and YouTube"

I think if I didn't have AI to edit it, I wouldn't be vlogging because editing would be such a painful and slow process for me and hiring someone to do it would be even more hassle for me!

items.content:
@iamsupersocks Tout cela est correct. Merci.

Sauf une chose : j'ai bien créé FAIR en 2013, y compris la branche parisienne en 2015, et montréalaise en 2017.
Mais j'en ai quitté la direction en 2018 pour devenir Chief AI Scientist: je me suis refocalisé sur la recherche (Self-Supervised Learning, JEPA, World Models, etc).
@AntoineBordes et @joellepineau étaient les co-directeurs de 2018 à 2023, jusqu a ce qu'Antoine parte pour Helsing et que Joëlle prenne la direction de FAIR.

Je n'ai jamais été impliqué dans les LLMs, ni pour la recherche (à FAIR), ni pour le développement (qui était dans le groupe de produit GenAI). J'applaudissais des gradins.

Mes seules contributions aux LLMs ont été de défendre Galactica (en octobre 2022) contre les attaques aux vitriol de la twittersphere, de promouvoir le projet Llama en interne (développé par une douzaine de chercheurs à FAIR-Paris, dont @GuillaumeLample et Timothée Lacroix), d'aider à convaincre Mark Zuckerberg de créer un groupe de produit autour de Llama (GenAI, créé début 2023), et de convaincre la direction de distribuer Llama-2 en open source/open weight.
Je n'étais pas du tout impliqué dans la direction de GenAI après sa création, préférant travailler sur la prochaine révolution: l'IA physique.

Si vous cherchez un responsable pour le déception qu'a été Llama-4, c'est plutôt la pression de sortir un produit (trop) rapidement, qui a conduit à un excès de conservatisme et un manque d'innovation de la part de l'équipe de GenAI. 
Mon avis est que l'équipe aurait dû prendre un peu plus de temps et intégrer les dernières techniques venant de la recherche à FAIR.
Mais ils n'en ont pas eu le loisir.

En particulier, conserver plus de pouvoir de décision quant aux choix techniques dans les mains des créateurs originaux de Llama à Paris, au lieu de déplacer les décisions à Menlo Park, aurait peut-être permis de conserver les meilleurs talents un peu plus longtemps et de produire de meilleurs résultats.

items.title: Long-running work in research, software, and operations often continues beyond a model’s context win...
items.content:
Long-running work in research, software, and operations often continues beyond a model’s context window, a single process, and the intervals when a person can supervise it. Simply extending context does not solve the problem: state and constraints can be lost during resets, goals can drift, and unchecked errors can compound. The article argues that before an agent can learn continually, its surrounding system—the “harness” that schedules, stores, checks, and directs work—must let it operate continuously without forgetting.

The article sets out an architecture for that purpose and reports a ten-day test of it. The architecture organizes work into levels that act on different time scales and keep short, durable summaries; uses a scheduled “tick” as the unit of autonomous action; records instructions, decisions, and progress in explicit files; and assigns work to models of different capabilities. Routine work starts with lower-cost models and moves to stronger models or a human only when review shows that escalation is needed. Checks, recovery procedures, and clear rules for when to stop or ask for help are built into the workflow.

items.content:
As LLMs are used more often to make sequential choices from incomplete information, their ability to balance trying alternatives against repeating known successes becomes a practical reliability concern. The article examines whether language itself—not just the rewards and choices in a task—shapes that balance. Its central conclusion is that seemingly irrelevant wording can steer an agent toward decisions that are either helpful or seriously mistaken.

The article introduces a “semantic bandit” test: a simple choice task in which three options have different, initially unknown rewards, while their names and the scenario are varied without changing the underlying reward structure. The researchers tested three language models across abstract, farming, and clothing-recommendation settings, comparing meaningful labels with random letter-and-number labels and measuring exploration and missed reward. Most main conditions used 10 runs; a separate test of how individual reward values affected exploration used 20. A conventional bandit algorithm provided a comparison point.

items.content:
Masked diffusion models can generate many text tokens in parallel, but their token-by-token predictions may miss relationships across a sentence. This can produce incoherent text, and has forced a trade-off between generation speed and quality. The article addresses whether sentence-level meaning represented in continuous vectors can guide a masked diffusion model to generate more coherent text quickly.

The article proposes CRoCoDiL, a method that combines continuous representations with a masked diffusion model. It jointly trains an encoder to turn text into a set of vectors and a guided decoder that uses those vectors to reconstruct text. It then tests two generation strategies: one generates a vector representation first and decodes it into text; the other also refreshes that guidance partway through decoding, using the partially generated text. Experiments use LLaDA, an 8-billion-parameter masked diffusion model, trained and evaluated on Python code. Training draws on 12 million programs for the decoder and 2 million sequences for the continuous generator; quality tests include held-out samples and comparisons against the standard LLaDA approach.

items.content:
Video models can make plausible predictions about motion and physical events, but strong benchmark performance alone does not show what physical information they represent internally. The article investigates whether these models build compact, reusable physical variables—like a conventional physics simulator—or instead rely on distributed representations tailored to particular tasks. This distinction matters for understanding model reliability and for deciding whether their internal workings can support interpretable scientific or practical applications.

The researchers analyzed frozen video encoders from two model families, V-JEPA 2 and VideoMAE-v2. They used layer-by-layer tests to see when physical information could be read from the models’ internal activity. Their evaluation combined videos in which objects behaved plausibly or violated basic physical expectations with a simulated ball dataset whose speed, direction, and acceleration were precisely controlled. They also tested whether targeted changes to attention mechanisms affected these abilities.

items.content:
Software engineering issues typically arrive as informal, human-written descriptions lacking automated tests that reproduce the reported problem. Creating dependable reproduction tests is vital for modern software engineering because it validates reported bugs, guides development under test-driven development methodologies, confirms that proposed code patches actually resolve the issue, and guards against regressions. However, automatically generating these tests using AI models is challenging. Reproduction tests must strictly exhibit a "fail-to-pass" behavior—failing on the pre-fix codebase to confirm the bug and passing on the post-fix codebase to confirm the resolution—all before the final resolving code patch has even been authored.

The article evaluates and demonstrates a new automated reproduction test generation and selection system named e-Otter++. The primary objective is to advance the state of the art in producing verified fail-to-pass reproduction tests directly from natural-language issue descriptions and existing codebases without having access to human-written resolving patches.

AI coding assistants promise faster software development, but enterprise teams still need to understand where they help, where they fall short, and what safeguards and capabilities are required for reliable use. The article examines how professionals across different roles use these tools, how they believe the tools affect their work, and what they want from future systems. It also places the findings alongside a review of 35 recent surveys of professionals and students.

The article’s main study is an online survey of 57 employees at one technology company, collected in May 2025. Respondents came from several business areas, including finance and operations, software, and research, and varied substantially in experience: 42% reported more than 20 years in software engineering, while 26% had fewer than five. The researchers analyzed responses about motivations, perceived benefits, changes to development practices, code retention, and desired features. They also reviewed and manually checked information extracted from 35 surveys published mainly in 2024 and 2025.

January 18, 2026 — Adamuz, Córdoba (46...
items.content:
Spain has had two high-speed train crashes in a single year:

January 18, 2026 — Adamuz, Córdoba (46 killed)

October 28, 2026 — Urda, Toledo (at least 69 killed and more than 30 are still unaccounted for)

Both crashes would have been avoided if the system had been designed to save lives, not costs.

In the former crash, the automated track-integrity system detected an anomaly (a voltage drop), but the threshold for triggering a maintenance call was set to reduce false positives that would result in "too high" maintenance costs.

In the latter crash, one electronic safety system failed, and the backup system wasn't equivalent to the failed one in terms of the kinds of issues it could detect, so it wasn't capable of signaling that two trains were occupying the same segment of track. This isn't a backup if it's not functionally equivalent to the failed system, so, again, cost savings are the reason for nearly a hundred people losing their lives.

When capitalists are given the right to decide what's safe, they will always choose saving money over saving lives. They obviously aren't using their own transportation systems.

items.content:
The Venom Below — From the Sterns of Warship! - by - Alisa - @ailsaharvey @HowItWorksmag 

From a warship’s stern to the seabed: A short journey for a weapon with a potentially long afterlife. Ailsa Harvey’s “What Are Sea Mines?” examines these submerged explosives, whose threat to ships and submarines can persist after the conflict that brought them into the water.

Picture a sea mine and the familiar horned sphere probably comes to mind. Yet that silhouette says little about the ingenuity concealed inside the casing. A passing vessel might betray itself through its magnetic signature, or through the sound of its engines. Depending on the mine, touching the hull is unnecessary. Contact is merely one means of activation.

There is considerable variety in their underwater dispositions. A bottom mine rests on the seabed; a moored mine occupies the water above it, suspended from an anchored tether. Drifting mines travel with the currents. The limpet dispenses with that separation altogether, attaching magnetically to a vessel’s hull.

Of these arrangement, the moored design is particularly striking in Harvey’s illustration. Buoyancy draws the spherical body upward, against the restraint of the heavy base. The tether fixes the distance between the two. What looks almost rudimentary is an exercise in opposing forces, with an explosive charge held in the path of maritime traffic.

The strangest episode in the account takes us well beyond the sea. Harvey recounts how a powerful solar storm in August 4, 1972 triggered magnetic sea mines near North Vietnam Area. This revealed an extraordinary vulnerability: disturbances associated with the Sun could activate weapons meant to detect ships. The minefield’s sensitivity extended, disastrously, beyond its intended quarry.

That episode gives the technology an unsettling dimension. Even without a ship in its vicinity, a mine could respond to changes in its environment. And when hostilities cease, the work beneath the surface remains unfinished. Detection and clearance must contend with explosives that carry no visible announcement of their presence.
